topic.title: Forming three equations from a context and interpreting solutions
topic.subject: further-maths
topic.examWeightHint: Unit 1 is one two-hour calculator paper of 100 marks, sat every Summer. The forming-and-solving question is the long one near the end of the paper, worth 12 or 13 marks, and it has appeared in every paper read: Summer 2018 Q10, Summer 2022 Q11, Summer 2023 Q11, Summer 2024 Q11 and Summer 2025 Q12. Its shape is fixed: two or three short parts that each form one equation or show that the information gives a printed one, worth 1 or 2 marks each, then an eight-mark part that solves all three with three labelled answer slots, then a final short part that does something with the answer — a rescaling, a reverse percentage or a conversion. The scheme pays for each equation, for each elimination, for each value, and for the final context step, with generous follow-through from a wrong equation onwards. An instruction to show clearly each stage of the solution is printed with the solving part, and the Teacher Guidance states that sole use of a calculator gains no marks.

Read every value as the thing it stands for before writing it down

Turn a total into an equation with the counts as coefficients, every letter included
Turn 'is d dearer than' into an addition, on the correct side
Turn 'is p% greater than' into a multiplier of 1 + p/100, on the correct side
Turn 'as many as ... together' and 'three times as many' into equations
Substitute a point into y = ax² + bx + c to get a linear equation in a, b and c
Derive a printed equation forwards, and reach it by dividing the whole equation by one number

sheet.howExamined: Unit 1 is one two-hour calculator paper of 100 marks, sat every Summer. The forming-and-solving question is the long one near the end of the paper, worth 12 or 13 marks, and it has appeared in every paper read: Summer 2018 Q10, Summer 2022 Q11, Summer 2023 Q11, Summer 2024 Q11 and Summer 2025 Q12. Its shape is fixed: two or three short parts that each form one equation or show that the information gives a printed one, worth 1 or 2 marks each, then an eight-mark part that solves all three with three labelled answer slots, then a final short part that does something with the answer — a rescaling, a reverse percentage or a conversion. The scheme pays for each equation, for each elimination, for each value, and for the final context step, with generous follow-through from a wrong equation onwards. An instruction to show clearly each stage of the solution is printed with the solving part, and the Teacher Guidance states that sole use of a calculator gains no marks.
traps: Writing a percentage comparison as an addition, so a p% rise becomes + p (Summer 2022 FM1 Q11, Summer 2023 FM1 Q11)
Writing a comparison the wrong way round, so the cheaper item's letter stands alone (Summer 2022 FM1 Q11)
Leaving a letter out of an equation, especially when its count is one (Summer 2025 FM1 Q12)
Starting a show-that at the printed equation and checking the information fits it (Summer 2023 FM1 Q11)
Multiplying instead of dividing to reach the printed form (Summer 2024 FM1 Q11)
Dividing only the left-hand side to reach the printed form
Mixing pounds and pence inside one equation

Reversing a percentage fall by adding the same percentage back on (Summer 2025 FM1 Q12)
Writing down a negative age, a negative count or an absurd price without comment (Summer 2018 FM1 Q10)

workedExamples.stem:
A café sells scones, coffees and bowls of soup.
A coffee costs 70p more than a scone. A bowl of soup costs 50% more than a coffee. An order of 2 scones, 3 coffees and 1 bowl of soup costs £12.25.
Find the price of each item.

steps.working: Let $x$ be the price of a scone, $y$ the price of a coffee and $z$ the price of a bowl of soup, all in pounds.
steps.decision: Define the letters first, with their unit. A scheme cannot give method marks for equations whose letters have never been named, and choosing pounds now stops pence appearing later.

options: Because the unit fixes what every later number means
Because the letters must be x, y and z
whyMenu.explain: Choosing pounds means 70p is written as $0.7$. Half the reported losses on this topic are a unit slip of exactly that kind.

steps.decision: "Dearer than" is an addition, and it is added to the cheaper item. The coffee is the dearer one here, so its letter stands alone.
A rise of 50% multiplies by $1 + \frac{50}{100} = 1.5$. A percentage is a percentage of something, so it can never be added as a number of pounds.

options: Because 50% of the coffee is 0.5 times its price
whyMenu.explain: Adding the percentage as money would price the soup at $£52.10$ or $£2.60$, depending on where the decimal point lands. Neither is what the sentence says.

steps.decision: One equation per sentence, and every letter that belongs in it written in. An order equation takes each count times that item's own letter.
Two of the three equations already give one letter in terms of another, so substitution is faster than elimination here. Pick the route the equations offer rather than the one you always use.
Back-substitute into the simplest equations you have, which are the two comparisons.

steps.working: Check in $(3)$: $2.8 + 6.3 + 3.15 = 12.25$. A scone is £1.40, a coffee £2.10 and a bowl of soup £3.15.
steps.decision: Finish in the context's own words and units. Three bare numbers are not an answer to a question about a café, and prices this size are also a sense check on the whole solution.

workedExamples.stem:
A printing firm's profits are $x$, $y$ and $z$ thousand pounds per order.
In March it completed 12 standard, 8 premium and 6 bespoke orders for a total profit of £78000.
(i) Show that $6x + 4y + 3z = 39$.
(ii) Given also that $2x + 3y + z = 18$ and $2x + y + 3z = 22$, find the profit on a standard order in pounds.

steps.working: The letters are in thousands, so the March total of £78000 is $78$ in the same units.
steps.decision: Put both sides in the same units before anything else. Thousands on the left and pounds on the right is the slip the reports name most often on this question.
This is the line the show-that is really asking for. Write it before you touch the printed form, because a show-that is marked on the derivation, not on the answer.

steps.working: Dividing every term by $2$ gives $6x + 4y + 3z = 39$, which is the printed form.
steps.decision: Compare your coefficients with the printed ones to decide the factor and its direction. The printed numbers are smaller, so the step is a division; multiplying moves away from them.

options: Because $12 \div 2 = 6$, and the same factor works on every term
Because the right-hand side is a round number
Because dividing always simplifies an equation
whyMenu.explain: One factor has to work on all four numbers, the right-hand side included. If it does not, the line above it is wrong.

steps.decision: Equations $(2)$ and $(3)$ both begin with $2x$, so one subtraction clears a letter with no scaling at all. Look for that before you start multiplying equations.

steps.working: Clearing $x$ from $(1)$ and $(2)$ as well and solving the pair gives $x = 2$, $y = 3$ and $z = 5$.
steps.decision: Same plan as any three-unknown system: the same letter out of two different pairs, then back-substitute.

steps.working: The letters are in thousands, so the profit on a standard order is $2 \times 1000 = £2000$.
steps.decision: Scale back. The question asked for pounds and the letters were defined in thousands, so the last line is a multiplication by $1000$. Examiners report this step forgotten after solving that was otherwise faultless.

twin.stem: Using the same three equations, write down the profit on a bespoke order, in pounds.

workedExamples.stem:
A curve has the equation $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ and passes through the points $(1, 6)$, $(2, 15)$ and $(3, 28)$.
Find the equation of the curve.

steps.working: The unknowns are $a$, $b$ and $c$, not $x$ and $y$.
steps.decision: Name what you are looking for before you substitute. Each point gives a pair of numbers to put in, and what comes out is an equation in the three coefficients.

options: Because $x$ and $y$ are known at each point, so only the coefficients are left
Because a curve always has three unknowns
Because $a$, $b$ and $c$ come first in the alphabet
whyMenu.explain: A point fixes $x$ and $y$. Substituting turns the curve's equation into a linear equation in the three coefficients, which is why three points are exactly enough.

steps.decision: Substitute $x = 1$ and $y = 6$, and work out $x^2$ as you go so the coefficient of $a$ is a number.

steps.working: From the other two points: $4a + 2b + c = 15$ and $9a + 3b + c = 28$
steps.decision: The coefficient of $a$ is $x^2$ each time, so it is $4$ and $9$ here. Writing $2a$ instead of $4a$ is the commonest slip in this kind of question.

steps.working: Every equation ends in $+ c$, so subtracting: $(2) - (1)$ gives $3a + 1b = 9$ and $(3) - (2)$ gives $5a + 1b = 13$.
steps.decision: The letter to clear picks itself: $c$ has a coefficient of one in all three equations, so no scaling is needed at all.

steps.working: Subtracting those two leaves $2a = 4$, so $a = 2$, then $b = 3$ and $c = 1$.
steps.decision: The two new equations are an ordinary pair, and the $b$ terms are equal, so one more subtraction finishes it.
Answer the question that was asked, which was for the equation rather than for three numbers, and test it at a point you did not use in the last step.

twin.stem: A curve $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ passes through $(2, 15)$. Write down the equation in $a$, $b$ and $c$ that this point gives.

items.stem:
Four quick checks on what this lesson is built from. None of them is the new work, so answer from what you already know.
A price of £2.1 rises by 50%. What is the new price?
items.skill: Prerequisite: a percentage increase as a multiplier

options.feedback: A rise of 50% multiplies by $1.5$, and $1.5 \times 2.1 = 3.15$.
That adds 50 pounds. A percentage is always a percentage of something, so it multiplies.
That adds 0.5 of a pound. The 50% is 50% of the £2.1, not a fixed amount.

items.stem: Bróna is $y$ years old. Aoife is 5 years older than Bróna. How old is Aoife, in terms of $y$?
items.skill: Prerequisite: writing a comparison in algebra

options.feedback: Older means more, so the difference is added to the younger sister's age.
That makes Aoife the younger one. Decide who is older before you choose the sign.
"Older than" is a difference, so it is added. Multiplying would be "5 times as old as".

items.stem: How many pence are there in £21.3?
items.skill: Prerequisite: converting between pounds and pence

options.feedback: Multiply by 100. Keeping one unit throughout an equation is what makes the coefficients whole numbers.
That multiplies by ten rather than by a hundred. There are 100 pence in a pound.
That multiplies by a thousand, which is ten times too many.

items.stem: The curve $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ passes through $(2, 15)$. What does the first term become when the point is substituted in?
items.skill: Prerequisite: substituting a value into a squared term

options.feedback: $x$ is squared before it multiplies $a$, and $2^2 = 4$.
The square has been missed. The term is $ax^2$, so the number that multiplies $a$ is $x$ squared.
That is the $y$-coordinate. It belongs on the other side of the equals sign.

items.stem: A bowl of soup costs 50% more than a coffee. Which equation says that?

options.feedback: A rise of 50% is a multiplier of $1.5$, and the soup is the dearer item.
That adds 50 pounds, pricing the soup at £52.1.
The multiplier is right and the two items have swapped places: it is the soup that costs more.

items.stem: A candidate writes $2x + 3y = 12.25$ for an order of 2 scones, 3 coffees and 1 bowl of soup costing £12.25. What is missing?
items.skill: Check every letter appears in the equation

options.feedback: A count of one still needs its letter written in. Examiners report omitted variables as a recurring loss on this question.
The order includes a bowl of soup, so its price belongs in the bill: $2x + 3y + z = 12.25$.
The unit was fixed when the letters were defined, so it does not appear again. The missing piece is a letter.

items.stem: Your equation is $12x + 8y + 6z = 78$ and the printed form is $6x + 4y + 3z = 39$. What is the step between them?
items.skill: Reach a printed form by scaling the whole equation

options.feedback: $12 \div 2 = 6$, and the same factor works on all four numbers.
The printed coefficients are smaller than yours, so multiplying moves away from them. This was the reported error on the 2024 paper.

options.text: Divide only the left-hand side by $2$
options.feedback: An equation stays true only when both sides change together, so the right-hand side is divided too.

items.stem: A show-that question prints the equation you have to reach. Where does the working start?
items.skill: Know which direction a show-that runs

options.text: At the information in the question, finishing at the printed line
options.feedback: The derivation is what carries the marks, so it has to run forwards. The printed line is your last line, never your first.

options.text: At the printed equation, checking that the information fits it
options.feedback: That is working backwards, and it gains nothing: examiners have said so in more than one series.

options.text: At the answers, substituting them into the printed equation
options.feedback: The answers are not known yet at this stage, and substituting a result is verification rather than derivation.

items.stem: The letters were defined in thousands of pounds and the solving gives $x = 2$. The question asks for the profit in pounds. What do you write?
items.skill: Scale the answer back into the context's units

options.feedback: Multiply by $1000$, because each unit of $x$ was one thousand pounds.
That is the value in the units the letters were defined in. The scaling back is a mark of its own, and it is the one most often forgotten.
The scaling has been applied twice. One multiplication by $1000$ is enough.

items.stem: A candidate solving for three ages reaches $x = 17$, $y = 22$ and $z = -2$. What should she do next?
items.skill: Sense-check the answer against its context

options.text: Go back and check the equations she formed
options.feedback: An age of -2 is impossible, and the elimination is usually sound in cases like this, so the fault is in the translation.

options.text: Write the three values down and move on
options.feedback: A negative age cannot be right. Examiners have noted candidates accepting meaningless values without comment.

options.text: Change the sign of the negative one
options.feedback: Changing an answer to make it look sensible leaves the equations wrong and the other two values wrong with them.

items.stem: A profit falls by 30% to £3500. What was it before the fall?

options.feedback: The fall leaves 70%, so divide: $3500 \div 0.7 = 5000$.
Adding 30% back on is not the reverse, because the percentage is of a different amount each time. Check forwards and it does not return to £3500.
That takes another 30% off. The answer has to be larger than £3500, because the profit fell to reach it.

items.stem: What does a page with three correct values and no equations on it earn in Further Mathematics?
items.skill: Know what an unsupported answer earns

options.text: Nothing, because the equations carry the method marks
options.feedback: The Teacher Guidance says the full development must be shown, and the reports repeat that calculator-only answers gain nothing.

options.text: Full marks, because the values are right
options.feedback: Most of the marks in a forming question are for the equations and the eliminations, not for the three numbers.
There is no half credit for an unsupported answer here; the instruction to show each stage is printed with the question.

context.setting: One sentence of a café's price list turned into an equation

parts.stem:
A café sells scones, coffees and bowls of soup.
Let $x$ be the price of a scone, $y$ the price of a coffee and $z$ the price of a bowl of soup, all in pounds.

A coffee costs 70p more than a scone.

Write down an equation in $x$ and $y$.

Answer ________

scheme.for: a comparison written as an equation with the 70p on the correct side
$y = x + 0.7$, or any equation equivalent to it such as $y - x = 0.7$

hints: Decide first which of the two is the dearer one; that is the one the extra is added to.
Every price in this question is in pounds, so 70p is $0.7$.
parts.workedSolution:
The coffee is the dearer of the two, so its price is the scone's price plus the difference.
In pounds the difference is $0.7$, which gives $y = x + 0.7$.
A check with the real prices: $1.4 + 0.7 = 2.1$.

commonErrors.feedback: That makes the scone the dearer of the two. Read the sentence again and ask which price the extra is added to: it is the coffee, so the coffee's letter sits on its own.
The comparison is the right way round, so the method mark stands. The prices are in pounds, so 70p is $0.7$, not $70$. Mixing pounds and pence gives a coffee at $£71.40$.

context.setting: A percentage comparison between two café prices

parts.stem:
A café sells scones, coffees and bowls of soup.
Let $x$ be the price of a scone, $y$ the price of a coffee and $z$ the price of a bowl of soup, all in pounds.

A bowl of soup costs 50% more than a coffee.

Write down an equation in $y$ and $z$.

Answer ________

scheme.for: the percentage turned into a multiplier, $1.5$
$z = 1.5y$, or any equation equivalent to it such as $2z = 3y$

hints: A rise of 50% multiplies a price by $1 + \frac{50}{100}$.
A percentage is always a percentage of something. Here it is a percentage of the coffee's price, not a number of pounds.
parts.workedSolution:
A rise of 50% multiplies by $1 + \frac{50}{100} = 1.5$.
The soup is the dearer item, so $z = 1.5y$.
A check with the real prices: $1.5 \times 2.1 = 3.15$.

commonErrors.feedback: The percentage has been added as a number of pounds. That would make the soup $£52.10$. A percentage multiplies; it never adds.
That adds $0.5$ of a pound, giving a soup at $£2.60$. The 50% is 50% of the coffee's price, so it has to be a multiplier.
The multiplier is right, so the method mark stands. It is the soup that costs more, so the soup's letter is the one on its own.

questions.solutionProgram: soup = coffee x 1.5 -> z = 1.5y; check 3.15 = 1.5 x 2.1

emphasis: an order turned into an equation

context.setting: One café order turned into an equation

parts.stem:
A café sells scones, coffees and bowls of soup.
Let $x$ be the price of a scone, $y$ the price of a coffee and $z$ the price of a bowl of soup, all in pounds.

An order of 2 scones, 3 coffees and 1 bowl of soup costs £12.25.

Write down an equation in $x$, $y$ and $z$.

Answer ________

scheme.for: each item's count multiplied by its own letter and the three terms added

hints: Count of an item times the price of that item gives what that part of the order costs.
All three letters belong in the equation, even the one whose count is one.
parts.workedSolution:
The scones cost $2x$, the coffees $3y$ and the soup $z$.
Adding them gives the bill, so $2x + 3y + z = 12.25$.
A check with the real prices: $2.8 + 6.3 + 3.15 = 12.25$.

commonErrors.feedback: The soup has been left out. Its count is one, so its term is simply $z$, and an equation missing a letter cannot be solved with the others.
That is the bill for one of each. The counts multiply their own letters, so the scones contribute $2x$ and the coffees $3y$.

questions.solutionProgram: order 2 scones, 3 coffees, 1 soup -> 2x + 3y + z = 12.25; check 2x1.4 + 3x2.1 + 3.15 = 12.25

emphasis: a sentence with no numbers in it

context.setting: A counting comparison in a jar of coins

parts.stem:
A charity jar holds twenty-pence coins, fifty-pence coins and one-pound coins.
Let $x$ be the number of twenty-pence coins, $y$ the number of fifty-pence coins and $z$ the number of one-pound coins.

There are as many twenty-pence coins as there are fifty-pence and one-pound coins together.

Write down an equation in $x$, $y$ and $z$.

Answer ________

scheme.for: the two smaller groups added together on one side

commonErrors.feedback: The two coordinates have swapped roles. The second number of the pair is the value of $y$, so it is the one on the right of the equals sign.

parts.stem:
Write down the equation that comes from the point $(2, 15)$.

Answer ________
hints: $x^2$ is $4$ here.
parts.workedSolution: Substituting gives $a(2)^2 + b(2) + c = 15$, which is $4a + 2b + c = 15$.

commonErrors.feedback: The first term carries $x^2$, so with $x = 2$ it is $4a$ rather than $2a$.

parts.stem:
Write down the equation that comes from the point $(3, 28)$.

Answer ________
hints: $x^2$ is $9$ here.
parts.workedSolution: Substituting gives $a(3)^2 + b(3) + c = 28$, which is $9a + 3b + c = 28$.

Set out every stage of your solution.

Set out every stage of your solution.

scheme.for: one unknown removed, by eliminating it from a pair or by substituting one of the given equations, for example $4a + 2b + c = 15$ minus $a + b + c = 6$
a correct equation in fewer unknowns
the working carried through to a single unknown

hints: Number the equations $(1)$, $(2)$ and $(3)$ before you touch them.
Every equation ends in $+ c$, so subtracting one from another clears $c$ at once.
Clear the same letter from a second pair, then solve the two equations you are left with.
parts.workedSolution:
Each equation ends in $+ c$, so subtracting clears it.
$(2) - (1)$ gives $3a + 1b = 9$, and $(3) - (2)$ gives $5a + 1b = 13$.
Subtracting those two leaves $2a = 4$, so $a = 2$.

commonErrors.feedback: That value comes from an equation whose $ax^2$ term was left out. Check that each of your three equations carries all three letters.

Answer ________
hints: One substitution is enough, and the other equation is then a free check.
parts.workedSolution: Substituting $a = 2$ into $3a + 1b = 9$ gives $b = 3$.

commonErrors.feedback: A negative coefficient is possible in general, and here it comes from a missing term rather than the algebra. Rebuild the equation from the point and try again.

Answer ________

findTheMistake.stem: Niamh is asked to show that a printing firm's March orders give $6x + 4y + 3z = 39$, where $x$, $y$ and $z$ are profits in thousands of pounds. The firm completed 12 standard, 8 premium and 6 bespoke orders for £78000. Her working:
studentWorking: That matches the 12 standard, 8 premium and 6 bespoke orders
So the printed equation is right
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Every line here is arithmetically true, and the whole thing still earns nothing, because it runs the wrong way.
Line 1 starts at the printed equation, which is the thing that was to be shown. Lines 2 and 3 then check that it fits the orders. That is verification, and a show-that asks for a derivation.
Examiners have made this point in more than one series: working backwards from the given equations gains no marks, however tidy it looks.
correction: The letters are in thousands, so the total is 78
findTheMistake.feedback: The same four lines in the other order would score everything. Start from the orders, reach an equation of your own, and let the printed line be the last thing you write.

findTheMistake.stem: Eimear is told that a bowl of soup costs 50% more than a coffee, where $y$ is the price of a coffee and $z$ the price of a bowl of soup, both in pounds. Her working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
Line 1 turns a percentage into a fixed amount of money, and everything after it follows honestly from that.
A percentage is always a percentage of something. Here it is 50% of the coffee's price, so it depends on $y$ and cannot be a number on its own.
Line 3 is where the reading should have failed: a bowl of soup at £52.10 beside a coffee at £2.10 is not a café anyone would recognise.
findTheMistake.feedback: The rule is short enough to hold on to: a percentage comparison multiplies, an amount of money adds. Put one real price into your equation before you move on, and a translation like this one stops at the line it is written.

findTheMistake.stem: Órla has solved a system for three sisters' ages, in whole years. Her working:
studentWorking: (2) y - x = 5 (Aoife is 5 years older than Bróna)
So Aoife is 17, Bróna is 22 and Ciara is -2
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong:
The elimination in line 4 is faultless, and it is faithfully solving the wrong system.
Line 2 has the comparison the wrong way round: it says Bróna is the elder, where the sentence in brackets beside it says Aoife is. The equation should be $x - y = 5$.
Line 5 is where it should have been caught. Ciara's age comes out as -2, and no one is -2 years old.
correction: Aoife is 17, Bróna is 12 and Ciara is 8
findTheMistake.feedback: The method marks for the eliminations stand, because the working is genuinely correct on her own equations. Read the three values as ages before you write them on the answer line: an impossible one sends you back to the sentence it came from, and that is a cheaper repair than it looks.

prompts.prompt: What are the five stages of a forming-and-solving question, in order?
prompts.answer: Define the letters with their units; form one equation per fact; derive any printed form by scaling the whole equation; solve by elimination; interpret the answer back in the context.

prompts.prompt: How do you write "b costs 50% more than a" as an equation?
prompts.answer: b = 1.5a, because a rise of 50% multiplies by 1.5.

prompts.prompt: How do you write "b costs 70p more than a" as an equation, when the prices are in pounds?
prompts.answer: b = a + 0.7. The amount is added, and it is written in pounds to match the letters.

prompts.prompt: In a show-that question, which direction does the working run, and why?
prompts.answer: Forwards, from the information to the printed line. The derivation is what carries the marks, so starting at the printed equation earns nothing.

prompts.prompt: Your equation and the printed one have the same shape but different numbers. How do you decide what to do?
prompts.answer: Compare a coefficient with the printed one. If the printed number is smaller, divide the whole equation by the factor; if larger, multiply. The same factor must work on every term, the right-hand side included.

prompts.prompt: The letters were defined in thousands of pounds. What is the last line of the solution?
prompts.answer: The scaling back: multiply each value by 1000 so the answer is in the units the question asked for.

prompts.prompt: Your solution gives a negative age, or a negative number of coins. What does that tell you?
prompts.answer: That one of the equations was formed wrongly. The elimination is usually sound, so go back to the sentences and check each translation, in particular which item a comparison makes the larger.

prompts.prompt: A curve $y = ax^2 + bx + c$ passes through three points. What are the three unknowns, and where do the equations come from?
prompts.answer: The unknowns are the coefficients a, b and c. Each point fixes x and y, and substituting them gives one linear equation in the three coefficients.

prompts.prompt: Why must every one of the three letters appear in the equation you form, even when its count is one?
prompts.answer: An equation missing a letter is an equation in two unknowns, so it cannot be solved with the others. Examiners report omitted variables as a recurring loss on this question.

prompts.prompt: How do you reverse a fall of 30%?
prompts.answer: Divide by 0.7, because the fall left 70% behind. Adding the percentage back on is not the reverse, since each percentage is of a different amount.

findings.asked: Form three equations from a context (one not given as 'show that'), then solve.
findings.wentWrong: The unscaffolded equation was often wrong (x + y - z = 55 was typical); 'show' equations were set out poorly; wrong equations led to huge or negative values that were not questioned.
findings.rule: Translate each sentence separately and check the answers make sense.

findings.asked: Translate phrases like 'dearer' and '50% greater' into equations, then solve.
findings.wentWrong: The phrase-to-algebra steps were often omitted; the solving was excellent; money notation was rarely used.

findings.asked: Derive three given equations from percentages, then solve.
findings.wentWrong: Fewer worked backwards from the given equations than before, but starting equations were wrong (percentage signs confused) and sides were divided by different numbers to force the printed form; solving was near perfect.
findings.rule: Divide the whole equation by one number to reach the printed form.

findings.asked: Form equations in thousands, solve, then interpret.
findings.wentWrong: Multiplying instead of dividing to reach each given equation; an error in (i) propagated; after solving, many forgot to multiply by 1000; calculator-only answers earned nothing.
findings.rule: If you scaled down to solve, scale back up at the end - and show the method.

findings.asked: Form and solve three equations from a currency context, then reverse a 40% decrease.
findings.wentWrong: Variables were omitted from equations; some worked backwards from the answers; arithmetic slips; calculator jumps with no working; fractional answers; the final reverse-percentage-and-conversion step was the worst-answered part of the paper.
findings.rule: Write all three unknowns in every equation they belong to, solve on paper, and handle the final context step separately.

insight.ruleToRemember: Define x, y, z with units; turn each sentence into one equation; reach a printed form by dividing the whole equation by one number and show that line; after solving, rescale, answer in context and sanity-check the values.
insight.aStarSignal: Forming an unscaffolded equation from comparative wording and finishing with a context step (rescaling, a reverse percentage, a conversion).

checks.detail: Marked back through the app's own engines (src/components/items/mark.ts onto numeric.ts, algebra.ts, points.ts and text-marking.ts) by scratchpad/fm1-batch-c/check-marking.mts: 1230 assertions over the four bundles' 82 question parts, 46 note gates and 35 note figures, all passing. checks.detail: Five contexts, each solved by Cramer's rule in scratchpad/fm1-batch-c/lib.mjs and each solution substituted back into all three of its own equations before printing: CAFE [[2,3,1,12.25],[1,2,2,11.9],[3,1,1,9.45]] -> [1.4, 2.1, 3.15]; AGES [[1,1,1,37],[1,-1,0,5],[0,1,1,20]] -> [17, 12, 8]; COINS [[1,1,1,48],[2,5,10,213],[1,-1,-1,0]] -> [24, 15, 9]; PRINT [[6,4,3,39],[2,3,1,18],[2,1,3,22]] -> [2, 3, 5] thousands, so [2000, 3000, 5000] pounds; QUAD through [[1,6],[2,15],[3,28]] -> [2, 3, 1]. checks.detail: Marked back through the app's own engines (src/components/items/mark.ts onto numeric.ts, algebra.ts, points.ts and text-marking.ts) by scratchpad/fm1-batch-c/check-marking.mts: 1230 assertions over the four bundles' 82 question parts, 46 note gates and 35 note figures, all passing. Every correct answer is fed in each natural spelling (a solution set as bare values, with "or", with the letter repeated, in either order and in braces; a coordinate pair as a tuple and as x = …, y = …; a numeric answer bare and with its unit written after it); every one of the 98 published common errors is fed in and must be refused as an answer, must match its own pattern and must surface its own misconception tag, and for every non-text spec the marks it awards must equal the marks its entry claims; every diagnostic distractor must carry a misconception; every text part is fed its OWN worked solution and must earn every key-word group; every gate is fed each accepted spelling, each distractor and nonsense. The note's shape is checked too: a hero block first with three lines and a lede inside 60 words, a gate after every video, a visual in every numbered section, a recap card, and a gate inside the closing panel. Error routes re-executed against the published JSON by scratchpad/fm1-batch-c/verify-published.mjs: 75 routes, 98 published common errors (49 numeric, 49 algebraic, 14 of those re-derived as a structural error applied to the part's own published answer), no unexplained value and none typed by hand. In this bundle: 16 questions over 39 parts, 12 gates, 9 note figures, longest teaching stretch 127 words and longest closing-panel stretch 230.
